$description: Interaction and information-architecture rules (FEAT-008, ADR-025). Each rule is in the SDK's own words and cites its sources (CONTRACT-005). Generated into @ux-builder/ui/catalogue.json by tools/gen-catalogue.mjs; checked by tools/check-rules.mjs.

priorities.name: Gate
priorities.protects: Structural prerequisites: other rules read their output, so nothing else can be judged until they pass.
priorities.ruleOfThumb: Fix first; a failure here makes later findings meaningless.

priorities.name: Safety and user control
priorities.protects: Prevents irreversible loss, unapproved actions, privacy breaches and deception, and keeps the person in charge of AI and agents.
priorities.ruleOfThumb: Wins over every lower level, even when it adds steps or friction.

priorities.name: Accessibility
priorities.protects: The WCAG 2.2 baseline and the rubric's accessibility baseline: everyone can perceive and operate the UI.
priorities.ruleOfThumb: Never traded for brand, layout or simplicity.

priorities.name: Task completion
priorities.protects: The rubric's task-effectiveness baseline: every task can be reached, walked and finished, including when things fail.
priorities.ruleOfThumb: A convention or polish rule that blocks a task loses.

priorities.name: Platform contract
priorities.protects: Theme, tokens, SDK components and host (embedded view) contracts that keep apps consistent and maintainable.
priorities.ruleOfThumb: Holds unless it causes a P0 to P3 failure; then fix the theme or SDK, not the app.

priorities.name: Interaction conventions
priorities.protects: Platform conventions for navigation, layout, modals, feedback and AI transparency.
priorities.ruleOfThumb: The default behaviour; bend it only for a higher-level rule.

priorities.name: Refinement
priorities.ruleOfThumb: Applies when nothing above is at stake.

clashOrder: Dependencies first: a rule is not judged until every rule it depends on passes.
The higher priority wins (P0 beats P1 … P6): satisfy the higher rule, then meet the lower one as far as possible.
At the same priority, the more specific rule wins (a narrower when, scope or appliesTo).
Still tied: an error beats a warning, and a warning beats info.
Still tied: record a decision (simplicity.delta-decided) naming both rules and why one was chosen.

rules.title: The blueprint follows its contract
rules.statement: A blueprint has the fields CONTRACT-005 requires, no unknown fields, unique screen IDs, and destinations that name existing screens.
rules.rationale: Every other check reads the blueprint; a malformed one would make their findings meaningless.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-005: blueprint

rules.title: Standing warnings are fixed or accepted on record
rules.statement: A blueprint warning carried past a checkpoint is either fixed or recorded in the blueprint as accepted, with the reason and who accepted it.
rules.rationale: 'Journeys cover error paths' stayed at 15–19 warnings across 28 runs, and an intended 'screen reachable' warning was never recorded as accepted. Warnings that are always present stop being read.
rules.scope: Before each checkpoint. Applies to: Blueprint

sources.title: Nygard (2011), Documenting Architecture Decisions

rules.title: Screens are built from catalogue patterns
rules.statement: Every screen names a pattern the installed SDK ships.
rules.rationale: A screen from a pattern inherits its layout, states and adaptation; an invented one inherits none of them.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-005: blueprint

rules.title: A phone-width bar holds at most five destinations
rules.statement: In an app that supports the compact size class, keep the top-level destinations to five; group the rest or move them to a drawer.
rules.rationale: A bottom bar or tab bar has room for only a few equal targets; more makes each too small to read and tap.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints
Apple HIG: Tab bars

rules.title: Navigation stays visible on wide screens
rules.statement: From the expanded size class, show primary navigation as a standing rail or side navigation, not behind a menu button.
rules.rationale: Wide windows have room for it, and hiding destinations makes people hunt for them.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints
Android Developers: Design for large screens

rules.title: Destinations are links; menus are for actions
rules.statement: Move between top-level destinations with navigation links; keep menu buttons for actions on the current page or item.
rules.rationale: People expect navigation to be visible, bookmarkable and announced as navigation; a menu hides it and changes its semantics.

sources.title: WAI-ARIA APG: Landmark regions

rules.title: Show one pane until there is room for two
rules.statement: Use one pane in compact and medium windows, two from expanded (a list beside its detail), and three only in extra-large ones.
rules.rationale: Splitting a narrow window makes both panes cramped; a wide one wastes space with a single pane.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints
Material 3: Canonical layout examples
Android Developers: Design for large screens

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Keep dense content in one pane at medium
rules.statement: At the medium size class, use two panes only for sparse content with clear actions, such as settings; keep dense lists and tables in one.
rules.rationale: Two dense panes in a tablet-width window reduce usability.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints

rules.title: Every screen has one main landmark
rules.statement: Every screen has exactly one main landmark holding its primary content, with header and navigation landmarks where those regions exist.
rules.rationale: Two expert screens had no main landmark and failed the first audit's responsive-web verdict. Landmarks let keyboard and screen-reader users skip straight to the content.
rules.scope: All screens. Applies to: All patterns

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: Landmark Regions

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Screens work in portrait and landscape
rules.statement: Content is not locked to portrait or landscape unless one orientation is essential, such as a piano app or a cheque scan.
rules.rationale: People with devices mounted on wheelchairs, or who cannot rotate a phone, are locked out of apps that force one orientation.
rules.scope: Mobile and tablet screens. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.4 Orientation

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Put what matters most where people look first
rules.statement: The screen's title, its most important content and its primary action appear at the top and start edge, within the first screenful at common sizes. Secondary information comes after it.
rules.rationale: People scan in an F-shaped pattern and often stop before scrolling. Content below the fold or at the far edge is easily missed.
rules.scope: All screens. Applies to: All patterns

sources.title: NN/g: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web
NN/g: Visual Hierarchy in UX

rules.title: Sticky bars leave room for the content
rules.statement: Sticky headers, footers, banners and chat buttons together take up no more than about a quarter of a phone screen, never cover focused elements or form fields, and collapse or hide while the person scrolls down.
rules.rationale: Stacked sticky headers, cookie banners and chat bubbles can leave a phone user only a sliver of the content they came for, and often hide the field or button they are trying to use.
rules.scope: Any fixed or sticky element. Applies to: Headers, footers, banners, floating buttons

sources.title: NN/g: Sticky headers, 5 ways to make them better
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)

rules.title: Layouts leave room for translation
rules.statement: Buttons, labels, tabs and navigation fit text that is 30% to 100% longer than English, and support right-to-left languages, without clipping or overlapping.
rules.rationale: Layouts designed around short English words break when translated into German, Finnish or Arabic, producing truncated buttons and hidden labels in the very markets a product is expanding into.
rules.scope: Products that are, or may be, translated. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: W3C Internationalization: Text size in translation

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Content does not jump once it has loaded
rules.statement: Space for images, data and late-loading content is reserved in advance, so that nothing moves under the person's pointer or finger after the screen appears.
rules.rationale: Layout shifts make people tap the wrong thing, sometimes a destructive one, and lose their place while reading.
rules.scope: Screens that load content asynchronously. Applies to: All patterns

sources.title: web.dev: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)

rules.title: Spacing comes from a scale and shows grouping
rules.statement: Spacing uses the theme's spacing tokens (a 4 or 8 px scale), and related items sit closer together than unrelated ones, so that groups are visible without boxes or lines.
rules.rationale: People read closeness as belonging together. Random spacing makes a screen look unfinished and makes groups ambiguous.
rules.scope: All screens. Applies to: All patterns

sources.title: NN/g: Proximity Principle in Visual Design
Material Design 3, Layout: spacing

rules.title: Use a modal only when it clearly helps
rules.statement: Present a task modally only when it needs focus or a decision before the person continues; otherwise keep it in the page.
rules.rationale: A modal takes people out of their context and must be dismissed before they can return.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: One modal at a time
rules.statement: Never open a modal on top of another, and never show more than one alert at once; close one before presenting the next.
rules.rationale: Stacked modals add clutter and make people lose track of the context they came from.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality
WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: A modal names its task
rules.statement: Give every modal a title that says what the task is, as its accessible name.
rules.rationale: People who enter a modal may not return to it straight away; the title keeps their place, and assistive technology announces it.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality
WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: A modal can always be dismissed
rules.statement: Give every modal an obvious way out (Cancel, Close or Done), and let Escape close it.
rules.rationale: A modal that is hard to leave traps people; keyboard users rely on Escape.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality
WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: Ask before discarding someone's work
rules.statement: When closing a modal would lose what the person entered, explain that and let them save, discard or keep editing.
rules.rationale: Losing typed work to a stray tap or swipe is a failure people remember.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: Keep modal tasks short, with one path
rules.statement: Keep a modal task brief; if it needs several steps, give them a single path and no buttons that could be mistaken for dismissing it.
rules.rationale: A long or branching task inside a modal feels like an app within the app and makes people forget how they got there.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: Dialogs take focus in and give it back
rules.statement: When a dialog or drawer opens, focus moves into it and stays there until it closes; when it closes, focus returns to the control that opened it.
rules.rationale: Without this, keyboard and screen-reader users keep tabbing through the page behind the dialog, and after closing it they are dumped at the top of the page.
rules.scope: Dialogs, drawers, full-screen overlays. Applies to: Modal

sources.title: W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: Dialog (modal) pattern
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3 Focus Order

rules.title: Don't cover the page with pop-ups on arrival
rules.statement: Newsletter sign-ups, app-install prompts, offers and surveys never open over content as soon as a page loads or the person starts scrolling. Use an inline or non-blocking banner, or show the offer after the person has done what they came for.
rules.rationale: Arrival pop-ups are among the most disliked web design patterns: they block the content people came for, and many dismiss them without reading. Search engines also rank pages lower when interstitials cover content.
rules.scope: Promotional, sign-up and survey prompts. Applies to: Landing pages, content pages

sources.title: NN/g: Pop-ups: 10 problematic trends and best practices
Google Search Central: avoid intrusive interstitials and dialogs

rules.title: Destructive actions are safeguarded
rules.statement: Give every destructive action a safeguard: Undo when the loss is expected and reversible, a confirmation only when it is unexpected or irreversible; never neither, and not both.
rules.rationale: Warning about expected deletions trains people to dismiss warnings; no safeguard at all loses data.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Feedback
WCAG 2.2: 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)

rules.title: Destructive actions look different and are never the default
rules.statement: A destructive action uses the danger style, is set apart from routine actions, and is never the default button or the one focused when a dialog opens; in a confirmation, focus starts on the safe choice.
rules.rationale: When Delete looks and sits like Save, or Enter triggers it, people destroy work by habit.
rules.scope: Any destructive action. Applies to: Buttons, dialogs, menus

sources.title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Alerts: destructive buttons are never the default
NN/g: Confirmation Dialogs Can Prevent User Errors (If Not Overused)

rules.title: Pressing twice never does it twice
rules.statement: Payments, orders, bookings and messages are sent once however many times the button is pressed. While the request runs, the button shows it is working ('Paying…') and ignores further presses, and the service treats repeats as the same request.
rules.rationale: On slow connections people press again when nothing seems to happen, and get charged or booked twice. Duplicate transactions are costly to unwind and destroy trust.
rules.scope: Any action that creates, sends or charges. Applies to: Forms, checkout, booking, messaging

sources.title: Stripe API: Idempotent requests
NN/g: Response times, the 3 important limits

rules.title: Repeated actions say which item they act on
rules.statement: When an action repeats on one screen (one per row or card), each instance has an accessible name that includes its item, for example 'Ask Priya Shah', and the visible label is contained in that name.
rules.rationale: Three buttons all named 'Ask this person' could not be told apart by screen-reader users, and the same ambiguity broke end-to-end test locators twice.
rules.scope: Lists, tables and card grids with per-item actions. Applies to: List, table, card grid

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6 Headings and Labels
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context)
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3 Label in Name

rules.title: Buttons say what they do
rules.statement: Button and menu labels start with a verb and name the result ('Save draft', 'Send invitation'), not 'OK', 'Submit', 'Yes' or 'Click here'.
rules.rationale: Specific labels let people act without reading the surrounding text, and make confirmations safe to answer.
rules.scope: All buttons and menu items, on the app's own screens (cards sent to a host are checked by card.action-titles). Applies to: Buttons, dialogs, menus

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System, Button: write button text that describes the action
NN/g: OK–Cancel or Cancel–OK?

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Buttons sit in the same place every time
rules.statement: Primary and secondary buttons follow one consistent order and position in every dialog and form footer, following the platform's convention.
rules.rationale: People learn where 'confirm' lives; moving it between screens causes mis-clicks.
rules.scope: Dialogs and form footers. Applies to: Modal, form

sources.title: NN/g: OK–Cancel or Cancel–OK?
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #4 Consistency and standards

rules.title: State buttons match the current state
rules.statement: A toggle or state-changing button's label matches the current state and the action it will take. It never offers to undo a state that is not in effect.
rules.rationale: A pause button read 'Take requests' when nothing was paused, telling the person the opposite of the truth.
rules.scope: Toggles and pause/resume controls. Applies to: Settings, status controls

sources.title: Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #1 Visibility of system status
NN/g: Toggle-Switch Guidelines

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Interactive things look interactive
rules.statement: Buttons look like buttons and links look like links (colour plus underline or another non-colour cue in body text), and non-interactive elements such as badges and headings do not look clickable.
rules.rationale: Flat, unmarked controls make people hunt for what they can do; clickable-looking decoration wastes clicks.
rules.scope: All screens. Applies to: Buttons, links, cards, badges

sources.title: NN/g: Beyond Blue Links: Making Clickable Elements Recognizable
WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color

rules.title: Avoid unexplained disabled buttons
rules.statement: Prefer leaving an action enabled and explaining what is missing when it is used. If a button must be disabled, the reason is shown next to it.
rules.rationale: A greyed-out button gives no clue what to do next, and disabled controls often have too little contrast to read.
rules.scope: Actions with preconditions. Applies to: Buttons, forms

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System, Button: avoid disabled buttons
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #1 Visibility of system status

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: Every action responds at once
rules.statement: Every click or tap shows a visible response within about a tenth of a second. An action that takes longer shows that it is working and cannot be triggered twice by mistake.
rules.rationale: Without a response, people click again, submitting twice or cancelling their first click.
rules.scope: All actions. Applies to: Buttons, forms

sources.title: Nielsen, NN/g: Response Times: The 3 Important Limits

rules.title: Show status where it belongs
rules.statement: Show the status of something next to it, passively; interrupt with an alert only for critical, actionable information.
rules.rationale: Interruptions lose their effect when they are used for unimportant news.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Feedback

rules.title: Say why a command cannot run
rules.statement: When an action cannot be carried out, say why and what to do, in text next to it.
rules.rationale: A control that silently does nothing looks broken.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Feedback

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: Status changes are announced
rules.statement: Messages that appear without a page change, such as 'Saved', '3 results', 'Added to cart' or an error count, are exposed as status or alert messages so screen readers announce them without moving focus.
rules.rationale: In single-page apps most feedback appears silently in place. Without an announcement, screen-reader users do not know their action worked and often repeat it.
rules.scope: Any in-place status, result count or error message. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.3 Status Messages

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: Say when the connection is lost, and keep the work
rules.statement: When the network drops, the product says so in place, keeps what the person has entered and either queues their actions to send later or explains which ones cannot be done offline.
rules.rationale: Silent failures on poor connections look like a broken product: people retry, lose input or assume an action went through when it did not.
rules.scope: Any product used on mobile or unreliable networks. Applies to: All screens, forms

sources.title: web.dev: Offline UX design guidelines

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: Empty screens explain and offer a first step
rules.statement: An empty list, inbox, dashboard or project says what will appear there, why it is empty now and offers the action that fills it, such as 'Create your first invoice'.
rules.rationale: A blank area with 'No data' gives new users no idea what to do next, so first-run empty states are where many people abandon a product.
rules.scope: Collections and dashboards that can be empty. Applies to: Lists, dashboards, inbox, first run

sources.title: NN/g: Designing empty states in complex applications

rules.title: Error pages help people get back on track
rules.statement: 'Page not found', 'Something went wrong' and access-denied pages say in plain words what happened, keep the product's navigation and offer next steps: search, home, the previous page or contact.
rules.rationale: A bare technical error page is a dead end that makes people think the whole product is broken, and they leave.
rules.scope: 404, 500, access-denied and maintenance pages. Applies to: Error pages

sources.title: NN/g: Improving the dreaded 404 error message
GOV.UK Design System: Page not found pages

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: Error messages explain and help
rules.statement: An error message says what happened in plain words, what the person can do next, and keeps their work. It does not blame the person, show raw codes alone, or use vague words like 'Something went wrong' without a next step.
rules.rationale: A clear message turns an error into a short detour; an unclear one ends the task.
rules.scope: Any error. Applies to: Alerts, banners, inline errors

sources.title: NN/g: Error-Message Guidelines
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #9 Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors
H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Long work is saved as people go
rules.statement: Long forms, editors and multi-step tasks save drafts automatically and show their save state ('Saving…', 'Saved 2 min ago', 'Couldn't save'). People can leave and return to where they were.
rules.rationale: Losing work to a crash, a closed tab or a lost connection is one of the most damaging experiences a product can create. A visible save state also removes the anxiety of wondering whether work is safe.
rules.scope: Forms or editors that take more than a few minutes. Applies to: Forms, editors, applications, multi-step flows

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.5 Re-authenticating (data is not lost)
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics

rules.title: Settings make clear whether they save on their own
rules.statement: Each settings screen uses one model: either changes apply immediately (toggles, with a brief 'Saved' confirmation) or they wait for a Save button, which is then always visible. The two are never mixed on one screen.
rules.rationale: When some settings save instantly and others need a button off-screen, people leave believing changes were saved when they were not.
rules.scope: Settings and preferences screens. Applies to: Settings

sources.title: NN/g: Toggle-switch guidelines
Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Settings

rules.title: Toasts are only for messages it is fine to miss
rules.statement: Brief notifications that disappear on their own (toasts, snackbars) carry only confirmations. Errors, warnings and anything needing action stay on screen until dismissed. Any timed message stays long enough to read and pauses while focused or hovered.
rules.rationale: A message that vanishes after three seconds is missed by anyone who looked away, reads slowly or uses a screen reader.
rules.scope: Transient notifications. Applies to: Toast, snackbar

sources.title: Material Design 3, Snackbar guidelines
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: Offer undo instead of asking 'Are you sure?'
rules.statement: Reversible actions such as archiving, moving, removing from a list or sending to the bin happen at once and offer Undo for a few seconds. When to confirm instead is decided by action.destructive-safeguard.
rules.rationale: Routine 'Are you sure?' dialogs train people to click Yes without reading, so they stop protecting anything. Undo lets people work quickly and still recover from a slip.
rules.scope: Reversible actions that remove or move something. Applies to: Lists, inbox, editors

sources.title: NN/g: Confirmation dialogs can prevent user errors, if not overused
Material Design 3: Snackbar guidelines
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics

rules.title: Confirm what happened and what happens next
rules.statement: After a significant action (submit, send, pay, publish), the screen confirms that it worked, gives any reference, and says what happens next.
rules.rationale: Without confirmation people repeat the action or call support to check that it went through.
rules.scope: Significant actions. Applies to: Confirmation, toast, banner

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System, Confirmation pages pattern

rules.title: Show something while content loads
rules.statement: Show placeholder content, such as a skeleton, as soon as a region starts loading; never leave it blank.
rules.rationale: An empty region reads as a broken app.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Loading

rules.title: Match the progress indicator to what is known
rules.statement: Use a determinate progress indicator when the duration is known and an indeterminate one when it is not.
rules.rationale: A bar that moves honestly helps people decide whether to wait.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Loading

rules.title: Screens of data handle empty, loading and error
rules.statement: A screen that shows a collection, a record or figures declares its empty, loading and error states.
rules.rationale: These states are where most data screens fail; a pattern supports them only when the screen supplies them.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Loading
Apple HIG: Feedback

heuristics: H9 Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors

rules.title: One primary action per page or dialog
rules.statement: Give each page region or dialog at most one primary (filled) button; make the others secondary or text buttons.
rules.rationale: When everything is emphasised, nothing is, and people hesitate over which action is the main one.

sources.title: Material 3: Buttons
Apple HIG: Buttons

rules.title: Touch targets are finger-sized
rules.statement: Under touch input, make every control at least the theme's touch-target size (44 points on Apple platforms, 48 dp in Material).
rules.rationale: Small targets cause mis-taps, especially for people with limited dexterity.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Layout
Material 3: States
WCAG 2.2: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Nothing is reachable only by hovering
rules.statement: Under touch input, never put content or actions where only hovering reveals them.
rules.rationale: Touch screens have no hover; what hover reveals is unreachable.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
Material 3: States

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Keyboard focus is always visible
rules.statement: Show a visible focus indicator on every focusable control, distinct from hover and selection.
rules.rationale: Keyboard users need to see where they are; state is shown in more than one way so it does not rely on colour alone.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 2.4.7 Focus Visible
Material 3: States

rules.title: Choices that act for the person start unselected
rules.statement: A checkbox, radio or list choice that contacts another person, sends a request, shares data or gives consent starts unselected; the person selects it.
rules.rationale: Pre-ticking the first colleague for an availability check was the usability assessment's only P1 finding: people send requests they did not mean to send. A pre-ticked box is also not valid consent.
rules.scope: Forms and selection lists. Applies to: Form, list selection, step prototype

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System, Radios: do not pre-select options; Checkboxes guidance
GDPR Recital 32: pre-ticked boxes do not constitute consent

rules.title: Shake and tilt actions have a button too
rules.statement: Anything triggered by moving the device, such as shake to undo or tilt to scroll, can also be done with a normal control, and motion triggers can be turned off.
rules.rationale: People with tremors trigger motion actions by accident, and people whose device is mounted cannot trigger them at all.
rules.scope: Any device-motion interaction. Applies to: Mobile apps

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.4 Motion Actuation

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Changing a setting never jumps somewhere else
rules.statement: Focusing a field or changing a dropdown, checkbox or radio never navigates away, submits a form or opens a new window on its own. Results that update in place are fine; changes of context need a button.
rules.rationale: A dropdown that navigates as soon as it changes makes keyboard users land on the wrong page while still browsing options, and surprises everyone else.
rules.scope: Form controls and filters. Applies to: Forms, filters, settings

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.2 On Input
WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.1 On Focus

rules.title: Single-letter shortcuts can be turned off
rules.statement: Keyboard shortcuts that use a single letter, number or symbol key can be turned off or remapped, or work only while the relevant component has focus.
rules.rationale: Speech-input users dictate words that fire stray shortcuts ('a' archives, 'd' deletes), triggering actions they never meant.
rules.scope: Products with keyboard shortcuts. Applies to: Inbox, editors, lists

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Tooltips and pop-overs stay put until dismissed
rules.statement: Content that appears on hover or focus can be dismissed with Escape without moving the pointer, can itself be hovered over without disappearing, and stays visible until the person moves away or dismisses it.
rules.rationale: Tooltips that vanish when the pointer moves towards them, or that cover content and cannot be closed, frustrate screen-magnifier users and anyone with a less precise pointer.
rules.scope: Tooltips, pop-overs, hover menus. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Everything works with a keyboard
rules.statement: Every action that can be done with a pointer can be done with the keyboard alone, in a logical order, and focus can always move away from any component. Custom widgets follow the keyboard patterns in the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices.
rules.rationale: Custom menus, date pickers and drag-and-drop built from plain divs often cannot be reached by keyboard. People who use a keyboard, switch or voice control are then locked out of the task entirely.
rules.scope: Any interactive component. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 Keyboard
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap
W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Every field has a visible label
rules.statement: Every form field has a visible label that stays visible while the person types and is tied to the field programmatically. A placeholder is never the label.
rules.rationale: 'Needed by' shipped without a visible label. People cannot tell what the field wants, and assistive technology has nothing to announce. The existing card.input-label rule covers cards only.

rules.title: Card action titles say what they do

rules.title: Navigation stays in the same place and order
rules.statement: Menus, search, account and other navigation that repeat across screens appear in the same place and in the same relative order on every screen.
rules.rationale: When navigation shifts between screens, people have to search for it again each time. People with low vision or cognitive disabilities, who rely on learned positions, are hit hardest.

rules.title: Help is always in the same place
rules.statement: Contact details, a help link, chat or a self-help option, wherever offered, appear in the same place on every screen, so people can find a human or an answer without hunting.
rules.rationale: Help that moves, or appears only on some screens, leaves people stuck at the point they most need it. WCAG 2.2 made this a Level A requirement.

rules.title: Back goes back, and keeps the person's place
rules.statement: The browser or system Back action returns to the previous view the person saw, with its scroll position, filters, tab and form input intact. Opening a modal, panel or step that feels like a new page adds a history entry so Back closes it.
rules.rationale: Breaking Back is one of the longest-standing web design mistakes and is common in single-page apps. People lose their search results or filters, start again or give up.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)

rules.title: Empty controls can be seen
rules.statement: In every appearance, the parts that show a control is there meet theme.contrast's 3:1 minimum against what surrounds them, in their resting states: an unchecked checkbox or radio outline, an off switch's track or thumb, an empty text field's border, bottom line or fill. The theme draws these from a control-edge token, never from the decorative border token used for cards and dividers, and check outlines are at least 1.5 px.
rules.rationale: Every Databricks-based theme drew unchecked checkboxes, off switches and empty fields with the decorative border token, so they were close to invisible; Material's filled fields blended into the page and Synaptiq's dark off switch faded out. People with low vision, or anyone on a bright screen, cannot tell an empty control is there, and a form looks like blank page.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: Checkboxes, radios, switches, text fields, selects, pickers

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast

rules.title: The focus ring is solid and clearly visible
rules.statement: The theme's focus indicator is a solid ring at least 2 px thick, with a 2 px offset, at 3:1 or more against both the control and the background, in every appearance. A soft or half-opacity halo may only be added on top of it, and a field's focus is never shown by a thin bottom bar alone.
rules.rationale: Four themes drew the focus ring at half opacity and Fluent showed field focus only as a 2 px bottom bar, so keyboard users lost their place. input.focus-visible requires an indicator; this rule sets what the theme's indicator must look like so every app inherits a usable one.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: All focusable controls

rules.title: Text people need to act on is never tiny
rules.statement: Field labels, hints, error messages and helper text use the theme's small size or larger, and the small size is at least 14 px. 12 px is kept for pills, badges and similar short tags, and nothing people must read to finish a task is set below that.
rules.rationale: Every theme let field errors and hints fall to 12 px, and Synaptiq set field labels in small capitals with a 12 px floor. These are exactly the words people need to fix a mistake, and text.readable-size covers body text only.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Field labels, hints, errors, helper text, captions

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 Resize Text
GOV.UK Design System, Type scale
Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Typography

rules.title: Theme names are checked as typed and kept
rules.statement: The theme builder checks a theme name as it is typed, says what is allowed, and saves the theme under the name entered.
rules.rationale: An invalid name was accepted, then the builder saved the theme under its own name; the person had to report it and ask for a rename, costing two corrections and one other turn.
rules.scope: Theme builder. Applies to: Theme builder

sources.title: Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #5 Error prevention
Wroblewski (2009), Inline Validation in Web Forms, A List Apart

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Every theme ships a designed dark appearance
rules.statement: Each theme defines a dark appearance with its own value for every colour, shadow and elevation token, rather than leaving dark to inverted or light-mode values. Contrast, status colours and shadows are rechecked in dark, not inherited.
rules.rationale: The Plain theme had no dark appearance at all, and Synaptiq's dark menus reused light-mode shadows. Apps that follow the system appearance then show a light island in a dark desktop, or dark surfaces with shadows that cannot be seen.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: All colour, shadow and elevation tokens

sources.title: Material Design, Dark theme
Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Dark Mode

rules.title: Buttons and fields line up
rules.statement: Buttons and fields that can sit side by side share one height at each density, on the 4 px grid (for example 36 or 40 px); larger standalone call-to-action buttons are a separate size. Their inner padding comes from the spacing scale, so a button's edge aligns with the field box beside it.
rules.rationale: Carbon (48 vs 40 px), Material (56 vs 40 px) and Synaptiq (48 vs 44 px) put mismatched buttons beside fields, Plain's buttons were 34 px off the grid, and four themes padded fields and buttons differently. Ragged rows look broken and slow scanning.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Buttons, text fields, selects, search bars

sources.title: Carbon Design System, Spacing
Material Design 3, Typography: type scale tokens

rules.title: The theme defines every component token
rules.statement: A theme sets the full component anatomy block (field, menu, check, switch, table, card, button and progress tokens) explicitly, on its spacing and radius scales, instead of relying on the SDK's generic fallbacks.
rules.rationale: Plain and Praxis left field, menu and table tokens undefined, so those components fell back to generic values that do not match the rest of the theme or sit on its grid.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Component anatomy tokens

sources.title: Design Tokens Community Group: Design Tokens Format

rules.title: The SDK takes every themeable value from a token
rules.statement: The shared SDK stylesheet hard-codes no value a design system would want to change: sizes (such as the small button height), disabled-state treatment, opacities and radii all come from tokens with sensible defaults, so each design system can set its own.
rules.rationale: The small button height was hard-coded for every theme, and disabled controls used a fixed 45% opacity. Carbon, Fluent, Material and Databricks each need different values, and the fixed opacity can make disabled text unreadable on some surfaces.
rules.scope: Shared SDK stylesheet (packages/ui/src/ui.css). Applies to: SDK components

sources.title: Design Tokens Community Group: Design Tokens Format

rules.title: The type scale has a steady step
rules.statement: Adjacent roles in the theme's type scale (small, body, lead, heading, title, display) step up by a steady ratio of about 1.125 to 1.25, so no two hierarchy roles share a size and there is no large jump between neighbours. Sizes are whole pixels.
rules.rationale: Seven themes had a flat or compressed middle: heading equal to lead, lead equal to body, or label equal to small; Material had a large gap between display and title. Screens built with these themes cannot show which text matters more.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Type scale tokens

sources.title: Material Design 3, Typography: type scale tokens
Carbon Design System, Type sets
NN/g: Visual Hierarchy in UX

rules.title: Text colour tiers are visibly different
rules.statement: The theme's text colour tiers (strong, default, muted, subtle) are visibly different steps from each other in every appearance, and each still meets theme.contrast. If two tiers cannot be told apart while both meet contrast, the theme retires one rather than shipping two that look the same.
rules.rationale: Databricks' muted and subtle text were the same colour, Plain's were almost identical, and Synaptiq's default and strong text matched in light. Designers then pick a tier for meaning that nobody can see, and the hierarchy collapses.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: Text colour tokens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
NN/g: Visual Hierarchy in UX

rules.title: Key colours clear contrast with room to spare
rules.statement: Accent, primary-action, status and subtle-text colours clear the WCAG minimum with a margin (about 4.7:1 or more for text-sized use, rather than exactly 4.5:1) in both appearances, and the primary action stays the strongest-contrast control on the page. theme.contrast stays the pass/fail gate; this rule flags colours sitting on the line.
rules.rationale: Praxis' light accent and subtle text sat at exactly 4.5:1, Img 8593's dark accent and Praxis V2's accents were marginal, Synaptiq's dark statuses were borderline, and Databricks' dark primary button looked low-energy. Anti-aliasing, opacity and small brand tweaks push such colours below the minimum without anyone noticing.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: Accent, structure, status and subtle-text tokens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast

rules.title: Structure and accent are different colours
rules.statement: The theme's structure colour (primary buttons, headings, chrome) and its accent colour (links, selection, focus) are clearly different tones in every appearance, so color.accent-means-action can be followed. A red brand colour is handled by color.red-reserved.
rules.rationale: UX Builder Databricks used the same violet for structure and accent, and Synaptiq's dark structure matched its accent. Headings then look clickable, and links, selection and primary buttons all compete for the same signal.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: Structure and accent colour tokens

sources.title: Material Design 3, Color roles
NN/g: Flat UI Elements Attract Less Attention and Cause Uncertainty

rules.title: Cards and menus stand out from the page
rules.statement: Cards, menus, popovers and dialogs separate from the page ground in every appearance, through a surface tone at least about 1.25:1 against the ground, a visible border, or a shadow tuned for that appearance. Dark mode uses its own stronger shadows (around 0.4 to 0.5 alpha) or lighter surfaces, and overlay shadows are soft (larger blur, moderate alpha) rather than heavy.
rules.rationale: Cards and menus barely separated in dark mode in five themes, disappeared on the light ground in Plain, Praxis and Databricks, and Carbon's dark overlay shadows were heavy. People cannot see where a menu ends or which content belongs together.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: Ground, surface, border, shadow and elevation tokens

sources.title: Material Design 3, Elevation
Carbon Design System, Themes: layering tokens
Material Design, Dark theme

rules.title: Theme fonts are available, or fall back on purpose
rules.statement: Each theme font is either licensed for web use and shipped with the SDK, or named with a metric-compatible fallback that is declared and documented. A theme that relies on a platform font (system-ui, Segoe UI) documents how it looks where that font is missing.
rules.rationale: Praxis' heading face depended on a licensed font, Fluent's Segoe UI is missing on macOS and Linux, and Plain's system-ui renders differently on each OS. Without a declared fallback, line lengths, wrapping and hierarchy change from one machine to the next.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Font tokens and font files

sources.title: MDN: font-family, generic and fallback families
Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Typography

rules.title: The theme offers a comfortable and a compact density
rules.statement: The theme defines a default density and a compact one. By default buttons and fields are at least 40 px, table rows about 48 px with 12 to 16 px cell padding, and cards padded 16 px on compact widths and 24 px on wider ones. Compact density (smaller controls, 40 to 44 px rows) is an opt-in that data-heavy patterns may use as their default.
rules.rationale: Fluent used 32 px controls everywhere, four themes crammed table cells next to roomy cards, Carbon padded cards only 16 px at every width, and Material's data screens were too sparse. One density cannot serve both forms and data tables.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Control, table, menu and card size and padding tokens

sources.title: Material Design, Applying density
Carbon Design System, Spacing

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Weights carry emphasis the same way in every appearance
rules.statement: Strong text and table headers use weight 600 or more, primary button labels 500 or more, and the same weights are used in light and dark. If dark text looks too heavy, the theme lowers its tone, not its weight.
rules.rationale: Praxis dropped bold to 500 in dark mode, Carbon set primary button labels at 400, and Material's table headers were not bold. Emphasis then disappears in one appearance, and primary actions read as plain text.
rules.scope: Every theme, light and dark appearance. Applies to: Font-weight tokens

sources.title: Material Design 3, Typography: type scale tokens
Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Typography

rules.title: Progress bars are thick enough to see
rules.statement: Progress bars are at least 4 px tall, 6 px when the progress is the main content, and their fill meets 3:1 against the track.
rules.rationale: Fluent's progress bar was 2 px tall, easy to miss on the page and hard to read at a glance.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Progress indicators

sources.title: Material Design 3, Progress indicators
WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast

rules.title: Corners come from a small radius scale
rules.statement: The theme uses a scale of three or four radii (for example 4, 8 and 12 px), each mapped to a role: checks, controls and toasts, cards and notices. Pills and buttons have clearly different shapes, such as fully round pills beside 8 px buttons.
rules.rationale: Four themes used five radii, two of them off-scale, and in Fluent and Material pills and buttons shared, or swapped, their rounding, so tags looked pressable.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Radius tokens

sources.title: Material Design 3, Shape: corner radius scale

rules.title: A published theme has its real name
rules.statement: Before a theme is shared or published, its theme and brand names are the real product or brand name, not a placeholder taken from a file or image name.
rules.rationale: The Img 8593 Databricks theme still carries a placeholder name taken from a screenshot file. People choosing a theme cannot tell what it is for.
rules.scope: Before a theme is shared or published. Applies to: Theme and brand metadata

sources.title: Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #2 Match between system and the real world
ux-builder FEAT-003: the guided brand builder

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: The app uses at most two type families
rules.statement: Inside the product, a theme uses one family for text and at most one more for headings and display. Brand faces may be used for display and title roles; marketing-only faces stay on marketing and hero pages.
rules.rationale: Synaptiq used three display faces in the app hierarchy, while Material replaced the brand faces with Roboto entirely. Too many faces look noisy; none of the brand's faces loses the brand.
rules.scope: Every theme. Applies to: Font-family tokens

sources.title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Typography
NN/g: Visual Hierarchy in UX

rules.title: Every turn of the person's is logged
rules.statement: Every message the person sends is logged with its kind, including clarifications and button presses that carried no content. If logging is declined, the agent explains once why it is needed, asks again, and reports the gap in the session's metrics.
rules.rationale: Two of the four session targets (meaningful turns, approvals before testing) are computed from the turn log. With turns missing, the 80% meaningful-turns target cannot be measured and approvals cannot be counted, so no guide change can be judged.
rules.scope: Guided session (ux-builder-design), every step. Applies to: Turn log (metrics.jsonl)

sources.title: ISO 9241-11:2018 Usability: definitions and concepts (efficiency and effectiveness need measured interactions)
Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu (2010), HEART framework: goals, signals, metrics

rules.title: Every attempt at a check is counted
rules.statement: An episode's outcome records every run of each check and how many failed, not only the runs after the last change.
rules.rationale: 'Checks to green' read 1 for an audit that took four tries and missed four contrast errors. A summary that hides the struggle cannot show whether the agent is improving.
rules.scope: Every trace episode. Applies to: Trace episode outcome

sources.title: Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu (2010), HEART framework

rules.title: The first prototype is marked when the person first tries one
rules.statement: The first-prototype milestone is recorded the first time the person clicks through anything clickable (a sketch, a skeleton, an exploratory or validated prototype). Other milestones, such as testing, are recorded when the activity happens, not when its kit is approved.
rules.rationale: The milestone was never marked in one session, was marked late in another (a clickable skeleton existed 20 minutes earlier) and 'testing' was recorded at test-kit approval in a third. The time-to-prototype target only means something if the milestone tracks what the person actually did.
rules.scope: Guided session, steps 1 to 7. Applies to: Design state milestones

sources.title: Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu (2010), HEART framework: pick signals that reflect the goal

rules.title: Time and approvals are measured over the whole session
rules.statement: Active time is measured from the person's first message, step 1 included. Approvals are counted once per turn of the person's, whatever the wording, and a message that holds two approvals counts as one turn.
rules.rationale: One session's own report gave 72 active minutes against 160 rebuilt from the transcript, and its approval count matched only by coincidence. Comparisons between guide versions are meaningless if the baseline is measured differently each time.
rules.scope: Guided session, metrics report. Applies to: Metrics report

sources.title: ISO 9241-11:2018 Usability: definitions and concepts

rules.title: A trace episode is open before anything changes
rules.statement: A trace episode naming the agent and model is open before any blueprint, screen, test or design-state change. Design-phase work is never left unscoped.
rules.rationale: All three sessions left design work 'unscoped', and one never opened an episode at all, so its trace recorded no agent, no model and no departures. Without episodes, agent quality cannot be measured.
rules.scope: Any change to the blueprint, screens, tests or design state. Applies to: Trace (.ux-builder/trace)

sources.title: Google PAIR Guidebook: Explainability + Trust (record what the system did and why)

rules.title: Departures and workarounds are recorded and told
rules.statement: Every departure from a guide rule and every workaround is recorded in the trace with its flag set on purpose, lists the alternatives considered, and is told to the person when it happens, not only in a later report.
rules.rationale: One trace recorded no departures against about twelve in the transcript; others left out chained commands, batched state changes and a batch approval disclosed only in the review. A trace that records none cannot show where the guide or the agent needs fixing.
rules.scope: Any departure, workaround or tool defect. Applies to: Trace decisions

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit, Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction: G11 Make clear why the system did what it did
Google PAIR Guidebook: Explainability + Trust

rules.title: The audit covers every screen and state
rules.statement: The UI audit runs on every screen and declared state in the blueprint, using paths taken from the blueprint. A run that covers fewer reports itself as incomplete, never as a pass.
rules.rationale: The first three audits in one session covered only the home page and reported warnings only; once all nine screens were audited, four contrast errors appeared at once. A pass on partial coverage is a false pass.
rules.scope: Every audit run. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: W3C WCAG-EM: Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology, step 3 (sample covers common pages, essential functionality and states)

rules.title: The usability assessment covers every journey and state
rules.statement: A usability assessment covers every journey-and-state pair the blueprint declares, or lists each pair it skipped and why. Its manifest's AI flags and allowed actions are generated from the blueprint, not written by hand.
rules.rationale: A hand-written manifest blocked every data-changing step and wrongly declared no AI, so the assessment covered 16 of 56 pairs.
rules.scope: Usability assessment (step 7). Applies to: Assessment manifest

sources.title: W3C WCAG-EM, step 3: include complete processes

rules.title: Unsubscribing takes one step
rules.statement: Every marketing email and push campaign carries a visible unsubscribe that works in one step, without signing in. Notification settings let people turn off each type separately rather than all or nothing.
rules.rationale: A missing or multi-step unsubscribe pushes people to mark messages as spam or delete the app. Major mailbox providers now require one-click unsubscribe from bulk senders, and the law in many markets requires a working opt-out.
rules.scope: Any marketing email, newsletter or push campaign. Applies to: Email, push, notification settings

sources.title: Google: Email sender guidelines, one-click unsubscribe
RFC 8058: one-click unsubscribe
FTC: CAN-SPAM Act compliance guide

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Notifications are few, relevant and well timed
rules.statement: Notifications are sent only for things the person cares about or must act on, low-priority ones are grouped into a digest, and nothing non-urgent is sent at night in the person's time zone.
rules.rationale: Over-notification is the main reason people turn notifications off entirely, after which even the important ones are missed.
rules.scope: Push, email, SMS and in-app notifications. Applies to: Notifications

sources.title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Managing notifications
Android Developers: Notifications overview

rules.title: Ask for permissions when they are needed, and say why
rules.statement: Notification, location, camera, contacts and similar permissions are requested only when the person starts a feature that needs them, never at launch. A short in-product explanation comes first, and the product still works if they say no.
rules.rationale: A permission request at first launch, before the person knows the product, is usually refused, and on most platforms a refusal is hard to undo. Asking in context with a reason gets more informed yes answers.
rules.scope: Any device or browser permission request. Applies to: Onboarding, feature entry points

sources.title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Privacy, requesting permission
Android Developers: Request runtime permissions
web.dev: Permission UX for push notifications

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Important transactions are confirmed in writing
rules.statement: Orders, bookings, payments, applications and account changes are confirmed on screen and by email or message with a reference number, what was agreed, what happens next and how to change or cancel it.
rules.rationale: Without a written record people screenshot pages, phone support or repeat the transaction to be sure it worked.
rules.scope: Orders, bookings, payments, submissions. Applies to: Confirmation screens, email

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Confirmation pages
Baymard Institute: order confirmation page

rules.title: An approval covers only what the person was shown
rules.statement: An approval covers only items the person was shown in a form they could read, and records the person's own words. A batch answer about an approach or theme does not approve the tasks, screens or alternatives behind it, and approving one item never silently approves another.
rules.rationale: 'Go with all four' approved a task, two screens and two alternatives that were never shown; 'Approve users' was recorded as approving the brief; and the agent tried three times to approve changed items without showing them. Approvals the person did not give make every later checkpoint unreliable.
rules.scope: Any approval in a guided session. Applies to: Review records

sources.title: Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #3 User control and freedom
ux-builder FEAT-018: the guided design loop

rules.title: Apply every change before recording the approval
rules.statement: All changes in one message of the person's are applied before any approval in that message is recorded, so the approval matches what is stored.
rules.rationale: An age-check rule was approved in the same message that changed it; the approval was recorded first, so the rule and the brief reopened at once and had to be approved again.
rules.scope: A message that both changes and approves items. Applies to: Review records

sources.title: Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #1 Visibility of system status

rules.title: Derived sections keep their approval
rules.statement: A section generated from items the person has just approved is carried: it updates, shows a visible note of what changed, and keeps its approval instead of being asked about again.
rules.rationale: Most brief re-approvals in all three sessions restated content approved minutes earlier in the users table, stories or rules. Asking twice for the same yes wastes turns and trains people to approve without reading.
rules.scope: A derived document changes because its source was approved. Applies to: Experience brief, coverage maps

sources.title: UK Government Design Principles: do the hard work to make it simple
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: One approval per question
rules.statement: Each approval question asks about one kind of item. Two approvals are never folded into one answer, such as a decision record plus a coverage map, or the brief plus a checkpoint.
rules.rationale: Two-in-one approvals happened three times in one session and once across four kinds in another. They keep turn counts down but make it unclear what the person agreed to.
rules.scope: Any approval. Applies to: Review questions

sources.title: Pew Research Center, Writing Survey Questions: avoid double-barrelled questions

rules.title: Settle open questions before asking for approval
rules.statement: An item is put up for approval only when no open question that would change it is outstanding. Recording an open question is not a change the person needs to approve.
rules.rationale: The brief was approved while four new questions were open and then reopened by their answers; elsewhere it was reopened just to record an open question. Asking too early doubles the approvals.
rules.scope: Any approval. Applies to: Brief, stories, rules

sources.title: Design Council, The Double Diamond: explore before converging

rules.title: Approve the brief once, at checkpoint 1
rules.statement: The experience brief is approved once, at checkpoint 1, after users, needs, stories and rules exist. Step 1 confirms only the product, the outcome and the constraints.
rules.rationale: The brief caused 2 of 2, 5 of 8 and 4 of 18 reopenings across the sessions, because it summarises things that do not exist yet in step 1. The fix was recommended after the first session but not made, and the second session repeated the problem.
rules.scope: Steps 1 to 3. Applies to: Experience brief

sources.title: ISO 9241-210:2019: iterate the design as understanding grows
Design Council, The Double Diamond

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Settle scope before approving stories
rules.statement: The scope review (what is in and out) is settled before stories are put up for approval.
rules.rationale: A story was approved, then the scope review changed its inputs and it had to be approved again.
rules.scope: Step 3 (Model tasks). Applies to: Stories, scope cuts

sources.title: ux-builder FEAT-018: the guided design loop

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Review stories beside their screens
rules.statement: A story, or a rule that shapes a screen, is reviewed beside a sketch of the screen it governs.
rules.rationale: A story approved as text reopened as soon as the person saw the door-check screen, and in another session every substantive change came from a prototype, none from a table. People decide visual questions by seeing them.
rules.scope: Steps 3 to 5. Applies to: Stories, rules, step prototypes

sources.title: ux-builder FEAT-018: the guided design loop

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Spend review effort where the person decides
rules.statement: Business rules, scope and screen states are reviewed in detail. Method artefacts (jobs, coverage maps, alternatives write-ups) are shown and confirmed by exception.
rules.rationale: Across sessions, people changed rules, scope and screens and approved jobs, coverage maps and alternatives without a single edit. Review time should follow the decisions people actually make.
rules.scope: Steps 2 to 5. Applies to: Review questions

sources.title: ISTQB Glossary: risk-based testing (direct effort by risk)

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Ask which row the person is least sure of
rules.statement: For a table longer than ten rows, the approval question also asks which row the person is least sure of, and records the answer as feedback on that row.
rules.rationale: Long tables (25 acceptance criteria) were approved in about 90 seconds with no feedback. When asked, the person gave useful confidence ratings. The question turns silent approval into a signal without adding a turn.
rules.scope: Approval of long tables. Applies to: Users, jobs, stories, rules

sources.title: Parasuraman & Manzey (2010), Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation

rules.title: Ads and sponsored content are clearly labelled
rules.statement: Paid placements, sponsored results, affiliate links and promoted posts carry a visible label such as 'Ad' or 'Sponsored' next to them, in text that is as easy to read as the content around it.
rules.rationale: Ads styled to look like ordinary results or articles mislead people about what is being recommended and why. Regulators in the US and EU require advertising to be identifiable as such.
rules.scope: Any paid, sponsored or affiliate placement. Applies to: Search results, feeds, lists, articles

sources.title: FTC: Native advertising, a guide for businesses
EU Digital Services Act (Regulation 2022/2065), Art. 26: advertising transparency

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Reviews and ratings are genuine and complete
rules.statement: Ratings and reviews come from real customers, are not filtered to hide negative ones and say how they were collected. Incentivised or verified-purchase reviews are labelled as such.
rules.rationale: People rely on reviews more than on product descriptions. Fake or cherry-picked reviews mislead them, and both the US and the EU now prohibit them.
rules.scope: Any rating, review or testimonial display. Applies to: Product, listing, profile pages

sources.title: FTC: The Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule, questions and answers
EU Directive 2019/2161 (Omnibus): verification of consumer reviews

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Urgency and scarcity messages are true
rules.statement: Countdown timers, 'only 2 left' and '12 people are viewing this' appear only when they reflect real, current data. A timer that resets on reload or a stock count that never changes is not used.
rules.rationale: Fake urgency was one of the most common deceptive patterns found across 11K shopping sites. It pushes hurried decisions and, once noticed, undermines trust in every other message the product shows.
rules.scope: Any timer, stock level or social-proof message. Applies to: Product, cart, checkout, booking

sources.title: Mathur et al. (2019): Dark Patterns at Scale, 11K shopping websites
FTC (2022): Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
UK CMA (2022): Online choice architecture: how digital design can harm competition and consumers

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Declining is worded neutrally
rules.statement: The option to decline an offer, upgrade or sign-up is a plain statement such as 'No thanks' or 'Not now'. It never mocks, guilts or frightens the person ('No, I don't like saving money').
rules.rationale: Guilt-tripping decline links pressure people into choices they would not otherwise make and leave a lasting sense of being manipulated. They are a recognised deceptive pattern in large-scale studies and regulator reports.
rules.scope: Any offer, upsell, sign-up or retention prompt. Applies to: Modal, banner, form

sources.title: Mathur et al. (2019): Dark Patterns at Scale, 11K shopping websites
Deceptive Patterns: Confirmshaming
FTC (2022): Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Opt-in choices are worded plainly
rules.statement: Every opt-in or opt-out is worded so that ticking or switching on means 'yes, do this'. No double negatives, mixed opt-in and opt-out boxes in one list, or wording that has to be read twice.
rules.rationale: Trick questions such as 'Untick this box if you would prefer not to not receive emails' lead people to agree to things they meant to refuse. They are a recognised deceptive pattern.
rules.scope: Any consent, marketing or data-sharing choice. Applies to: Forms, sign-up, checkout, settings

sources.title: Deceptive Patterns: Trick wording
Mathur et al. (2019): Dark Patterns at Scale, 11K shopping websites
FTC (2022): Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Saying no is as easy as saying yes
rules.statement: Any consent, cookie or tracking prompt offers a decline option on the same layer, with the same prominence and the same number of clicks as accept. Nothing optional is switched on before the person chooses, and changing their mind later is as easy as the first choice.
rules.rationale: Cookie banners with a bright 'Accept all' and a buried 'Manage options' are the most common deceptive pattern people meet. Regulators treat unequal choices as invalid consent, and the person ends up sharing data they never meant to share.
rules.scope: Any consent, cookie, tracking or data-sharing prompt. Applies to: Banner, modal, settings

sources.title: GDPR Art. 7(3): withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it
CNIL: cookies guidelines, refusing must be as easy as accepting
EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns

rules.title: The total price is shown from the start
rules.statement: The first price shown includes every mandatory fee and charge. Optional extras, taxes that vary by address and delivery costs are named as such and shown before the person commits, never revealed for the first time at the last step.
rules.rationale: Extra costs are the top reason people abandon checkout (40% of abandoners in Baymard's 2026 survey), and drip pricing is banned in a growing number of markets. A surprise total feels like a trick even when it is legal.
rules.scope: Any screen that shows a price people pay. Applies to: Product, cart, checkout, booking

sources.title: Baymard Institute: Cart abandonment rate statistics (2026)
UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024: drip pricing
FTC (2022): Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

rules.title: Paid extras are added only when chosen
rules.statement: Insurance, donations, warranties, subscriptions and other paid extras start unselected and are never added to a basket or order automatically. Each is added only by the person's own action.
rules.rationale: 'Sneak into basket' charges people for things they did not choose, and EU law already requires express consent for any extra payment. Pre-selected extras are discovered on the receipt and turn into refunds and complaints.
rules.scope: Any optional paid add-on. Applies to: Cart, checkout, booking, sign-up

sources.title: EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU, Art. 22: additional payments need express consent

rules.title: Privacy settings start at the most private option
rules.statement: Settings that share personal data, location, activity or a profile with others start at their most private value. People widen sharing themselves, and each option says who will see what.
rules.rationale: Most people never change defaults, so a public-by-default profile or location share exposes them without a real choice. Data protection law requires privacy by default.
rules.scope: Any setting that shares personal data or visibility. Applies to: Settings, profile, onboarding

sources.title: GDPR Art. 25: data protection by design and by default
EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns

rules.title: People can delete their account themselves
rules.statement: A product that lets people create an account also lets them start account deletion from inside the product, in settings where they would look for it. The screen says what will be deleted, what is kept and why, and when it takes effect.
rules.rationale: Both major app stores require in-app account deletion, and people have a legal right to erasure in many regions. Hiding deletion behind email or support requests is a common failure and a frequent cause of store rejection.
rules.scope: Any product with user accounts. Applies to: Settings, account

sources.title: Apple App Review Guidelines 5.1.1(v): account deletion
Google Play: account deletion requirements
GDPR Art. 17: right to erasure

rules.title: Cancelling is as easy as signing up
rules.statement: A subscription, membership or recurring payment can be cancelled in the same channel and with no more steps than it took to start. A retention offer may be shown once and is skippable; the cancel path never requires a call, chat or hidden page.
rules.rationale: Hard-to-cancel subscriptions are among the most reported dark patterns: an international review of 642 subscription sites found about three in four used at least one. They erode trust and expose the business to enforcement.
rules.scope: Any recurring payment, subscription or membership. Applies to: Account, billing, settings

rules.title: Free trials say when they will start charging
rules.statement: When a free trial turns into a paid plan, the sign-up screen states the date and amount of the first charge. A reminder is sent a few days before it, with a direct link to cancel.
rules.rationale: Trials that silently convert into payments ('forced continuity') are one of the most common subscription complaints. People feel tricked even when the terms were technically shown.
rules.scope: Any free or discounted trial that converts to a paid plan. Applies to: Sign-up, checkout, billing, email

rules.title: Respect a 'no' and don't keep asking
rules.statement: Prompts to rate the app, turn on notifications, upgrade or install the app are shown rarely, never mid-task, and a 'No' or dismissal is remembered for a reasonable period.
rules.rationale: Repeated prompts interrupt work and are classed as a deceptive pattern ('nagging') by European regulators. Rating prompts shown at random moments also produce lower, less useful ratings.
rules.scope: Rating, upgrade, permission and install prompts. Applies to: Modal, banner

rules.title: People can take their data with them
rules.statement: People can download the data they put into the product, such as their content, history and contacts, in a common, machine-readable format, from their account settings.
rules.rationale: Data lock-in is a reason people hesitate to commit to a product, and the right to data portability is law in many regions.
rules.scope: Products that store user-created data. Applies to: Settings, account

rules.title: Video has captions and audio has a transcript
rules.statement: Every video with speech or meaningful sound has accurate captions, and every audio-only recording has a transcript. Auto-generated captions are reviewed before publishing.
rules.rationale: Many people watch video with the sound off, and deaf and hard-of-hearing people cannot use media without captions at all. Unreviewed automatic captions often get names and key terms wrong.
rules.scope: Any video or audio content. Applies to: Media player, content pages

rules.title: Images have useful text alternatives
rules.statement: Every informative image has alternative text that conveys its purpose, not its file name; decorative images are marked as decorative so they are skipped.
rules.rationale: Missing alternative text is found on more than half of top home pages, so screen-reader users miss product photos, diagrams and icon-only content.
rules.scope: Any image, icon or illustration, on the app's own screens (cards sent to a host are checked by card.image-alt). Applies to: All screens

rules.title: Nothing plays sound on its own
rules.statement: Video and audio never start playing with sound unless the person asked. Any media that does auto-play starts muted and has a visible pause control.
rules.rationale: Auto-playing sound startles people, drowns out screen readers and is embarrassing in shared spaces. It is one of the quickest ways to make someone leave a page.
rules.scope: Any video, audio or animated media. Applies to: Media player, content pages, ads

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.2 Audio Control
Google Search Central: avoid intrusive interstitials and dialogs

rules.title: Colour is never the only signal
rules.statement: Status, errors, required fields, selection and chart series are shown by text, an icon, a pattern or position as well as colour.
rules.rationale: About one man in twelve has a colour-vision deficiency, and colour disappears in greyscale printouts and bright sunlight. A red border alone does not tell everyone that a field is wrong.
rules.scope: Any state or category shown by colour. Applies to: Status badges, form errors, charts, legends

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color
WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast

rules.title: Red is reserved for errors, warnings and destruction
rules.statement: Red, and hues close to it, is used only for errors, critical warnings and destructive actions. If the theme's brand primary is red, primary buttons, links, selection and focus use a non-red token instead, and the theme keeps a separate danger colour that is clearly distinct from the brand.
rules.rationale: People read red as 'stop, something is wrong, or this will delete something'. A red Save button or a red selected row makes routine actions look dangerous and real errors invisible among them.
rules.scope: Any screen; especially themes whose brand colour is red. Applies to: Buttons, links, selection, status, alerts
