rules.title: Status colours mean one thing everywhere
rules.statement: Each status has one colour and icon across the app: success green, warning amber, error red, information blue or neutral. Status colours are never used for decoration, branding or categories.
rules.rationale: When green means 'done' on one screen and 'Marketing team' on another, people stop trusting colour and have to read every badge.
rules.scope: Any status indicator. Applies to: Badges, alerts, banners, table cells

sources.title: Material Design 3, Color roles
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics: #4 Consistency and standards

rules.title: The accent colour signals what can be clicked
rules.statement: The theme's accent or link colour is kept for interactive elements. Headings, labels and decorative text do not use it.
rules.rationale: If static text shares the link colour, people click things that do nothing and miss the things that do.
rules.scope: Any screen. Applies to: Links, buttons, headings, labels

sources.title: NN/g: Beyond Blue Links: Making Clickable Elements Recognizable

rules.title: Motion is brief, purposeful and can be turned off
rules.statement: Animation explains a change (where something came from or went), lasts no more than about 300 ms and honours the system's reduce-motion setting. Flashing is covered by motion.no-flashing.
rules.rationale: Large or long motion causes nausea for people with vestibular disorders, flashing can trigger seizures, and slow transitions make every task feel slower.
rules.scope: Any animation or transition. Applies to: All patterns

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold
NN/g: The Role of Animation and Motion in UX

rules.title: Nothing flashes more than three times a second
rules.statement: No content, including video, animation and loading effects, flashes more than three times in any one second, unless the flash is small and below the general and red flash thresholds.
rules.rationale: Rapid flashing can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy. It is one of the few accessibility failures that can cause physical harm.
rules.scope: Any animation, video or visual effect. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold

rules.title: Moving content can be paused
rules.statement: Carousels, tickers, auto-updating feeds and animations that start automatically and last more than five seconds have a visible pause or stop control. Carousels do not auto-advance by default.
rules.rationale: Auto-advancing carousels move on before people finish reading, distract people with attention difficulties and are rarely clicked beyond the first slide. Reduced-motion settings alone do not help everyone who needs to stop movement.
rules.scope: Any automatically moving, blinking or updating content. Applies to: Carousels, banners, feeds, tickers

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide
Nielsen, 10 usability heuristics

rules.title: Charts have a text or table equivalent
rules.statement: Every chart has a short text summary of what it shows and access to the underlying numbers as a table. Series are told apart by labels, patterns or markers, not only by colour.
rules.rationale: Charts are images to screen readers and colour-only series cannot be told apart by people with colour-vision deficiencies, so the insight a chart carries is lost.
rules.scope: Any chart or data visualisation. Applies to: Dashboards, reports

sources.title: W3C WAI: Complex images tutorial
WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color

rules.title: Dates, numbers and money are unambiguous
rules.statement: Dates, times, numbers and currency are formatted for the person's locale; dates are unambiguous ('2 Nov 2026', not '02/11/26'); relative times ('3 hours ago') also give the exact time on demand; units and currency are always shown.
rules.rationale: '02/11/26' means different days in different countries, and a figure without a unit or currency invites costly misreadings.
rules.scope: Any date, time, number or amount. Applies to: Tables, details, forms

sources.title: GOV.UK Style Guide: dates and numbers

rules.title: Charts show data honestly
rules.statement: Bar and area charts start their value axis at zero; every axis is labelled with its unit; time scales are evenly spaced; and the chart type fits the comparison being made.
rules.rationale: Truncated axes and unlabelled units exaggerate small differences, leading people to wrong conclusions and damaging trust once noticed.
rules.scope: Any chart. Applies to: Dashboards, reports

sources.title: FlowingData: Bar chart baselines start at zero

heuristics: H2 Match between system and the real world

rules.title: Dashboards lead with the few numbers that matter
rules.statement: A dashboard opens with a small set of key figures tied to the person's goals, each compared with a target or the previous period, before any detailed charts.
rules.rationale: Dashboards that show every available metric with equal weight make people hunt for what matters, and they stop opening them.
rules.scope: Dashboards and overview screens

sources.title: NN/g: Dashboards: making charts and graphs easier to understand

rules.title: Tables are built for scanning and comparing
rules.statement: Numbers are right-aligned with consistent decimals and units in the header; text is left-aligned; headers stay visible while scrolling; and tables with more than about 20 rows offer sorting, filtering or search and show a row count.
rules.rationale: Aligned figures can be compared at a glance, and long tables without sort or filter force people to read every row.
rules.scope: Data tables. Applies to: Table

rules.title: Long lists let people act on many items at once
rules.statement: Lists and tables where people routinely act on several items offer row selection, select-all and bulk actions, and say how many items are selected.
rules.rationale: Without bulk actions, archiving or tagging fifty items means fifty repetitions, which wastes time and invites mistakes.
rules.scope: Lists and tables of actionable items. Applies to: Lists, tables, inbox

sources.title: Carbon Design System: Data table usage, batch actions

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Errors appear at the field and say how to fix them
rules.statement: A validation error is shown next to its field, in text as well as colour, says what is wrong and how to fix it, and is announced to assistive technology. When validation runs is covered by form.validate-on-leave.
rules.rationale: An error far from its field, or one that only turns a border red, leaves people guessing; errors that fire while someone is still typing feel like nagging.
rules.scope: Forms with validation, on the app's own screens (cards sent to a host are checked by card.input-error). Applies to: Form

rules.title: Fields use the right type and autocomplete
rules.statement: Each field uses the input type and autocomplete value for its data (email, tel, numeric, date, name, address), so that phones show the right keyboard and browsers can fill it in.
rules.rationale: The right keyboard and autofill cut typing and errors, and help people with motor or memory impairments.
rules.scope: Forms. Applies to: Form

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose

heuristics: H7 Flexibility and efficiency of use

rules.title: Never ask for the same information twice
rules.statement: Information the person already gave in the same process is filled in or offered for selection, such as 'Billing address same as delivery'. They are asked again only when re-entry is essential, for security or because the old value is no longer valid.
rules.rationale: Re-typing information is tedious for everyone and a real barrier for people with motor or memory impairments. It also introduces mismatches between two copies of the same data.
rules.scope: Multi-step forms and processes. Applies to: Forms, checkout, onboarding

rules.title: A failed submit leads to an error summary
rules.statement: When a form is submitted with errors, a summary at the top lists each one and links to its field, and focus moves to that summary.
rules.rationale: On a long form, people otherwise press Submit, see nothing happen and do not know where the problem is.
rules.scope: Forms with more than a few fields. Applies to: Form

rules.title: Never clear what the person entered
rules.statement: Entered values survive validation errors, server errors, and going back and forward between steps. Only fields that must be cleared for security (such as a password) are emptied.
rules.rationale: Retyping a whole form because one field was wrong is one of the most common reasons people give up.
rules.scope: Forms and multi-step flows. Applies to: Form, wizard

rules.title: Let people check their answers before submitting
rules.statement: A long or consequential form ends with a summary of every answer, grouped as asked, each with a 'Change' link that returns to that question and then back to the summary.
rules.rationale: Mistakes in a long application, booking or claim are expensive to fix after submission. A summary catches typos and wrong choices while they are still free to correct.
rules.scope: Multi-step or consequential forms. Applies to: Applications, checkout, booking, claims

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Check answers pattern

rules.title: Ask only for what is needed, and say why
rules.statement: Every field in a form is needed for the task or clearly optional. Sensitive or surprising questions, such as phone number, date of birth or gender, say why they are asked and how the answer will be used.
rules.rationale: Each extra field adds effort and drop-off, and checkouts commonly ask for nearly twice the fields they need. Asking for personal data without a reason feels intrusive and conflicts with data-minimisation law.
rules.scope: Any form. Applies to: Forms, sign-up, checkout

rules.title: Fields with a limit show how much is left
rules.statement: A text field or area with a character or word limit says so in its hint and counts down as the person types. Text over the limit is kept and flagged, never cut off.
rules.rationale: Limits found only on submit, or text silently truncated, force people to rewrite and can lose the end of what they wrote.
rules.scope: Fields with length limits. Applies to: Forms, messages, bios

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Character count

rules.title: Forms have no Reset or Clear-all button
rules.statement: Forms do not include a Reset or Clear button beside Submit. Where clearing is genuinely useful, such as filters, it is a secondary link with Undo.
rules.rationale: Reset buttons are almost never wanted and are easily pressed by mistake in place of Submit, wiping everything the person typed.
rules.scope: Forms. Applies to: Forms

sources.title: NN/g: Reset and cancel buttons

rules.title: Required and optional fields are marked
rules.statement: Whether a field is required is shown in its label, the same way throughout the app: mark the optional ones when most are required, and explain any asterisk once at the top.
rules.rationale: People should not discover what was required by submitting and failing.
rules.scope: Forms. Applies to: Form

rules.title: Forms run in a single column
rules.statement: Form fields are laid out in one column in the order people answer them. Only closely related short fields (such as city and postcode) share a row.
rules.rationale: Multi-column forms make people skip fields and zig-zag between columns; one column gives a single clear path to the end.
rules.scope: Forms. Applies to: Form

sources.title: NN/g: Website Forms Usability: Top 10 Recommendations

rules.title: Accept data in the formats people type
rules.statement: Fields accept common variations (spaces and dashes in phone and card numbers, upper or lower case in codes, leading or trailing spaces) and normalise them, instead of rejecting them.
rules.rationale: Rejecting '020 7946 0000' because of the spaces blames the person for the system's strictness.
rules.scope: Forms. Applies to: Form

rules.title: Check fields after people finish them, not while they type
rules.statement: Inline validation runs when the person leaves a field or submits, never on the first keystroke. A field already marked wrong clears its error as soon as it becomes valid.
rules.rationale: Errors that appear mid-word ('Invalid email' after typing 'j') feel like scolding and distract people from finishing. Errors that wait until submit force people to hunt back through the form.
rules.scope: Forms with inline validation. Applies to: Forms

rules.title: Names and addresses fit people everywhere
rules.statement: Name fields accept any characters, including accents, apostrophes, hyphens and single names; use one full-name field unless the parts are genuinely needed. Address forms adapt to the country chosen and don't require a postcode or state where none exists.
rules.rationale: Forms that reject 'O'Brien', 'Zoë' or a single name, or demand a ZIP code from a country without one, tell people they are not welcome and stop them completing the task.
rules.scope: Forms that ask for names, addresses or phone numbers. Applies to: Sign-up, checkout, profile

rules.title: Password fields offer Show password
rules.statement: Every password field has a 'Show' toggle so people can check what they typed. When creating a password, it is entered once, not twice.
rules.rationale: Masked passwords cause typos, especially on phones, and the 'confirm password' field doubles the effort without catching much.
rules.scope: Password entry and creation. Applies to: Sign-in, sign-up, password reset

GOV.UK Design System: Password input

rules.title: Multi-step tasks show progress and allow going back
rules.statement: A task split across steps shows where the person is (step 2 of 4, or named steps) and lets them go back without losing answers. The review before submitting is covered by form.check-answers.
rules.rationale: Without progress people cannot judge how long is left; without a way back they cannot fix an earlier answer.

rules.title: Pick the control that fits the choice
rules.statement: Use radio buttons for one choice from up to about six options, checkboxes for several choices, a switch for an instant on/off setting, and a dropdown or searchable list only for long option lists.
rules.rationale: Visible options can be compared at a glance; a dropdown hides them behind an extra click and is hard to use on phones.
rules.scope: Forms and settings. Applies to: Form, settings

rules.statement: Field labels are placed above their fields, with any hint text between the label and the field.
rules.rationale: Top-aligned labels are the fastest to scan and survive narrow screens and translated text that grows longer.

rules.title: Pick the date input that fits the date
rules.statement: Dates people know, such as a date of birth or a passport date, are typed into day, month and year fields. Calendar pickers are kept for choosing near-future dates, such as bookings, where seeing the weekday matters.

rules.scope: Any date entry. Applies to: Forms

rules.title: Signing in never depends on memory or puzzles
rules.statement: Password and code fields allow paste and password-manager autofill, and one-time codes use a single field that accepts a pasted or auto-filled code. Sign-in never relies on a puzzle, image selection or transcription test unless an alternative that needs no such test, such as a passkey or an email link, is offered alongside it.

rules.title: Time limits are warned and can be extended
rules.statement: Before a session or task times out, the person is warned at least 20 seconds ahead and can extend it with a single action. If the session does end, what they entered is kept and restored after they sign in again.
rules.rationale: Silent timeouts wipe out long forms and checkouts, and hit hardest those who need more time: people using assistive technology, reading in a second language or interrupted mid-task.

rules.title: Fixes from testing are retested or flagged
rules.statement: Fixes made after sessions with people are retested with at least one person, or recorded as assumptions to check, naming the stories they changed.
rules.rationale: Eight fixes changed five stories after three sessions and were not retested. Fixes can introduce new problems; untested ones must at least be visible as open risk.

rules.title: Offer real alternatives, not only a recommendation
rules.statement: A decision is offered with at least one genuine alternative and its trade-off. When the person has taken every recommendation so far, the guide notes this at the next checkpoint and asks which decision they are least sure of.
rules.rationale: Every decision in one session matched the agent's recommendation, and drafted answers were accepted wholesale in another. That fits good recommendations and deference equally; a challenge question tells them apart.

rules.title: Offer a clickable sketch early
rules.statement: A clickable sketch of the main journey is offered as soon as the intended experience is agreed, aiming for 30 active minutes, and is refined through steps 2 to 5. Open questions that would not change the sketch do not delay it.
rules.rationale: First prototypes took 63, 68 and about 148 active minutes against a 30-minute target. In every session the person's substantive changes came from looking at screens, so the earlier a screen exists, the earlier those changes happen.
rules.scope: Guided session, after the intended experience (step 1). Applies to: Step prototype, journey skeleton

rules.title: Step prototypes use real components, empty
rules.statement: Step prototypes are drawn with the SDK's real components in their empty state: inputs empty with hint text, guidance as static text, and sample data only where content is displayed, such as lists and results.
rules.rationale: The drawing template drew every line of a form as a text box, so guidance appeared as an input and sample data as values, causing a correction and a session finding. Low fidelity is fine; wrong fidelity misleads.
rules.scope: Step prototypes (steps 1 to 5). Applies to: Step prototype, wireframe

rules.title: An empty search result offers a way forward
rules.statement: A search or filter that returns nothing repeats what was searched, says why there may be no results, and offers next steps: a spelling correction, related terms, removing a filter or browsing a category.
rules.rationale: A bare 'No results' page is a dead end, and people often conclude the product does not have what they want and leave, even when it does.
rules.scope: Any search or filtered list. Applies to: Search results, lists, tables

rules.title: Search forgives typos and synonyms
rules.statement: Search matches misspellings, plurals, synonyms and the words people use, not just exact product or system names. It searches the fields people expect, such as names, descriptions, IDs and categories.
rules.rationale: Exact-match search returns nothing for 'tshirt' when the catalogue says 'T-Shirt'. People blame themselves, then the product, and leave without finding what was there.

rules.title: The search and filters in use stay visible
rules.statement: On a results page the search term stays in the search box, and every active filter is shown as a removable chip with a 'Clear all'. The result count updates as filters change.
rules.rationale: When the query disappears and filters hide in a closed panel, people forget why they see the results they see and cannot tell how to widen them.

rules.title: Make search a visible box where search matters
rules.statement: In content-heavy products where search is a main way in, search is an open text box in the header, not hidden behind an icon, and is in the same place on every screen.
rules.rationale: Hiding search behind a magnifier icon reduces how often it is used; people looking for search scan for an empty box.
rules.scope: Products with large catalogues or content. Applies to: Header

rules.title: Answer buttons send complete answers
rules.statement: Every answer button sends a complete message. An answer that needs detail (which item, what change) opens a text field instead of sending a sentence that ends in a colon.
rules.rationale: 'Bring one back' and 'Change the plan' were sent with nothing after them, and each needed a follow-up question.

rules.statement: Before offering an action (moving the work to a folder, installing a tool), the guide checks whether it is already done and does not offer it if so.
rules.rationale: Two sessions offered to move the work to a folder of the person's choosing when it was already in their Documents folder, once twice.

rules.title: Say when a tool is not available
rules.statement: When the person asks for a tool, connector or format the session cannot reach, the guide says so and offers the nearest working option before attempting a workaround.
rules.rationale: A Google Sheets request without a Sheets connector led to an upload detour and a failed first upload, about four turns spent on no design. Image export failed for want of a browser in another session.

rules.title: Batch related low-risk decisions
rules.statement: Related low-risk decisions (approach, modality, frame, theme) are asked together in one question, with a recommended default for each. Approvals are never batched this way.
rules.rationale: Batching approach, modality, frame and theme cut steps 4 to 6 from 29 to 12 active minutes. The same batch also approved unseen items, so it must stay a decision, not an approval.

rules.title: Show visual choices side by side
rules.statement: Visual choices such as themes or layout alternatives are offered as side-by-side previews on the app's own screens.
rules.rationale: The person chose a theme quickly once released themes were shown side by side; describing them in text would rely on memory.

rules.title: Help appears where the question arises
rules.statement: Hard fields, unfamiliar terms and complex settings carry short hint text or an expandable explanation right beside them, with a link to fuller help that opens without losing the person's work.
rules.rationale: People rarely leave a task to read documentation; when the answer is not where the question arises they guess, make mistakes or contact support.
rules.scope: Complex fields, settings and terms. Applies to: Forms, settings

rules.title: Essential information is never hidden in a tooltip
rules.statement: Information people need to complete a task, such as format rules, prices, fees or consequences, is shown on the page. Tooltips are only for supplementary detail.
rules.rationale: Tooltips are invisible until discovered, unreliable on touch screens and easy to miss, so anything critical hidden there might as well not exist.
rules.scope: Hints, fees, rules and warnings. Applies to: All screens

sources.title: NN/g: Tooltip guidelines

rules.title: Onboarding is short, skippable and can be found again
rules.statement: Intro tours and carousels can be skipped from the first screen, take no more than a few steps and can be replayed from help. Teaching happens in context, when the person first meets a feature, rather than up front.
rules.rationale: People skip or forget up-front tutorials; studies show they want to start using the product. Forced tours delay the first success and teach features before they matter.
rules.scope: First-run experiences and feature tours. Applies to: Onboarding, empty states, help

rules.title: Follow the platform's own conventions
rules.statement: On each platform, the product uses its native patterns for navigation, back behaviour, system gestures, sharing, pickers and alerts, rather than imposing one platform's patterns on another.
rules.rationale: People learn conventions from every other app on their device. A bottom tab bar where Android users expect predictive back, or an iOS-style alert on Android, makes the product feel wrong and slows people down.
rules.scope: Native and cross-platform apps. Applies to: All screens

rules.title: Pages meet a speed budget on ordinary devices
rules.statement: On a mid-range phone and a typical mobile connection, the main content appears within 2.5 seconds (LCP) and the page responds to input within 200 ms (INP) for at least 75% of visits. The budget is checked before release.
rules.rationale: Products are usually designed and tested on fast laptops, but most people use them on mid-range phones. Slow pages lose visitors and make every other design decision feel broken.
